items.text: Armor Piercing. The weapon or round bypasses the target's RES entirely. PROT still rolls -- AP does not make armor irrelevant; it makes the flat damage reduction irrelevant.
The weapon affects all targets within the listed radius of the point of impact rather than a single target. One attack roll affects everyone in range. Does not benefit from ACC bonuses.
The weapon causes the Bleeding condition on a successful hit.
The weapon sets the target on fire: ongoing damage each round until extinguished or the source is removed. Stacks with Energy damage when both are present.
Can be concealed on the person without detection by visual inspection or standard security checks. Specialized scanning or a successful Perception check against a defined threshold may reveal it.
Causes the Disoriented condition across its area of effect. Deals no damage. Affects all targets in range including allies.
Can perform a Disarm maneuver instead of dealing damage. Declare before the attack roll; a hit knocks the target's weapon free, automatically. Choose damage or disarm, not both.
On a killing blow, the target leaves no recoverable remains. The damage itself is not necessarily greater -- the permanence of the outcome is.

Disrupts electronic systems and cybernetic implants on hit. Minimal against standard targets; against heavily augmented targets or electronics, the EM pulse effect triggers separately from the damage.
Sets the impact area on fire, causing Burning to all targets in the affected zone until extinguished.
Can knock a target prone instead of dealing damage. Declare before the attack roll; a hit knocks the target down, automatically. Choose damage or knockdown, not both.
Requires a bipod, hardpoint, or vehicle mount for effective use. Firing without one: BOD Essence Check, success fires at −4 ACC, failure means the weapon is uncontrollable.
Produces no recoil on discharge. The ACC bonus applies to both Single and Burst fire, not just Single.
Designed for incapacitation rather than harm. Descriptor only -- the weapon's damage value (or lack of one) determines the mechanical effect.
The weapon's effect is determined by the equipped arrowhead or bolt type rather than the platform itself.
Deals Massive damage, to vehicles and structures and to people alike.
Produces no ballistic or acoustic signature detectable by standard means. Firing from hidden does not automatically reveal the attacker; the ambush bonus applies every round they remain undetected.
Creates an obscurement cloud blocking line of sight within its area for a GM-determined number of rounds.
Discharges across a cone, affecting multiple targets with one roll. Treated as an Area attack; no ACC bonus.
Causes the Stunned/Shocked condition on a successful hit.
Emits a burst of ultraviolet radiation dealing Withering damage specifically to undead and vampiric targets. Non-supernatural targets in range are unaffected by the UV component.
Does not behave predictably. Roll 1d4 to determine the actual effect when used.

Experimental or hybrid systems carry a risk of malfunction. On a botched attack roll, roll on the Volatile Misfire table (1: no effect; 2-3: jam, one Action to clear; 4: misfire, 5 damage ignoring armor, then jams).

Creates a zone of particulate matter converting all damage dealt to lycanthropes and their kindred within the area into Withering damage for the duration. Non-supernatural targets are unaffected by the cloud itself.

Damage of this type cannot be regenerated supernaturally -- it must heal at the natural rate regardless of the target's normal recovery. The damage amount is not necessarily greater; the permanence is.

Sustained fire across an area rather than at a target. Declare the zone: until the start of the firer's next turn, that ground is Difficult Terrain. No attack roll and no damage; the rounds are aimed at the space, not at anyone in it. Whether a target gets hit is a matter of cover and line of sight, as ever. What it costs them is the ability to get anywhere useful.

The weapon detonates at a point and catches everything within the radius: allies, enemies, bystanders and objects alike. The attack is made against the place, at Difficulty 10. Everyone caught Scrambles on a REF Essence Check at TN 8, TH 2, and the Threshold rises by one for every five meters of radius beyond the first five. Damage is the same for all of them; the Scramble decides what it costs. A lobbed blast needs no line of sight and reaches a target in Full Cover. A cone starts at the wielder and reaches only what the wielder can see.
Vehicle armor doesn't stop it, so it deals full damage to vehicles. Against a person it's the weapon's AP and damage that count, nothing extra.
The weapon reaches as far as its Reach column says. The tag marks a reach that's unusual for its kind; it adds nothing to the number.

parts.text: CRANK is the gray market's job board, on every device in NYTE City. Your rep is your record there: one job at a time, and it doesn't fade. Abandoning a contract is the one thing that follows you. Walking away from a client who broke it first isn't abandoning it, and costs nothing.

parts.title: The Job Generator
parts.text: Roll d10 on each column or choose manually. Five rolls give you a complete contract — a job type, a client, a target, a location, and a complication that will make it interesting. Not every element needs to drive the scene equally. Sometimes the complication is the whole job. Sometimes the location tells you everything.
parts.footText: The tables don't know the crew's tier, but you do, and the client column does most of the scaling for you. A small business owner's extraction pulls a cousin out of a bad apartment; a megacorp executive's pulls a defector out of a tower. Read every entry at the size the client can afford, and reroll anything that doesn't fit.

parts.title: Job Type
rows: Move something from one place to another. Legal, illegal, or dangerous — the package doesn't come with a label.
Get someone out. Whether they want to come is a separate question.
Steal data, sabotage a facility, or gather intelligence without being noticed.
Hack a system, plant something in it, or wipe something out of it.
Move illegal goods across a border or through territory that doesn't want them moved.
Keep something or someone safe. The threat isn't always obvious at the start.
Take something from somewhere it's being kept.
Remove a target. The contract specifies low-profile or high-profile. The target rarely cooperates with either.
Find a missing person, locate an item, or uncover something someone wants buried.
Get into a high-risk facility and come back out. Whatever's inside is worth the attempt — probably.

parts.title: Client
rows: Wants protection, a debt collected, or a competitor handled. Budget is limited; desperation is not.
Needs muscle, product moved, or a message delivered. Will pay in Skrip if they pay at all.
Wants it handled quietly and completely. No loose ends.
Needs evidence buried, a rival framed, or something retrieved before anyone asks questions.
High pay, high risk. Expect at least one layer of deception built into the contract.
Aims to disrupt corporate or government control. Pays what they can. Believes in what they're doing.
Black ops framing, minimal details, complete deniability. The paperwork doesn't exist.
Needs something done discreetly. The stakes are personal, which makes them unpredictable.
Unusual requests, unconventional payment methods, and ethical complications the client may not recognize as such.
Every posting is anonymous, but most give their client away through what they want and how they ask. This one doesn't. The job is real. The client is a question mark.

parts.title: Target
rows: Well-guarded, well-connected, and carrying information worth more than the posted rate.
Experienced and paranoid. Has their own crew.
Hard to find, harder to trust, and probably already knows you're coming.
Cyberware, weapon system, or AI component. Multiple parties want it.
The contents are unknown until they're not. Could be worth more than the contract.
Enormous fallout if the job goes loud. The client is counting on it not going loud.
Armed, dangerous, and backed by people who will take the loss personally.
High demand from multiple directions. Someone else is already moving on it.
The obstacle is digital. Getting through it is a technical problem until it isn't.
No description. No manifest. Just a location and a pickup.

parts.title: Location
rows: High-tech security, layered access, and staff trained to notice things that don't belong.
Off the books. Biological or chemical risk is possible. Nobody official knows it exists.
Gang-controlled, unpredictable, and full of people who've learned to stay out of other people's business.
Getting in requires a plan. Getting out requires a better one.
Loud, chaotic, and full of eyes. The noise is cover. So is everyone else.
Elite security, controlled access, and an owner who expects to be untouchable.
Traders, fixers, and competing interests in a space where everyone is watching everyone else.
Plenty of cover. Time pressure is almost always a factor.
The job happens in the digital layer. Physical security is someone else's problem — until it isn't.
Empty on paper. Rarely empty in practice.

parts.title: Complication
rows: The client is setting the crew up. The question is whether they figure it out before or after.
The location is locked down in ways the intel didn't mention.
Another team is working the same job. Their contract may or may not align with the crew's.
Someone with a badge shows up at exactly the wrong moment.
The job isn't what the posting described. The gap between what was promised and what's true is the real problem.
The client wants something beyond what the contract states. Whether that's a problem depends on what it is.
The window is hours, not days. Everything else adjusts accordingly.
More opposition than the tier suggested. Someone upgraded the threat level and didn't update the posting.
Completing the job cleanly means making a choice about who else gets caught in it.
Something not human is involved. It may be incidental. It may be the whole job.
